solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Muscles required with farm vehicle? He may produce shorter version

parts.note: abs are abdominal muscles
the farmer's towing vehicle

explanation.surface: A farmer wonders whether driving a tractor demands strong muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hangs on the farm picture, but the definition is the second half: someone who makes abstracts.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstractor writes abstracts, condensed summaries of longer documents.

clue.text: Sweet pastry, ornament in source of honey

indicators.note: in means placed inside the other word

parts.note: bees make honey
an ouch is an old word for a brooch or jewelled clasp

explanation.surface: A sweet pastry decorated with an ornament dipped in honey.
explanation.walkthrough: Ornament looks like decoration on the pastry, but it is an archaic word for a brooch or clasp.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouchée is a small puff-pastry case, often filled with something sweet or savoury.

clue.text: Walter's relation a couple of times put up with bishop

indicators.note: in a down entry, put up means written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: bis means twice
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A relative visited twice and put up with a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter is Sir Walter Scott, who used sibb, an old word for a kinsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibb is an archaic Scots word for a relative or kinsman, used by Walter Scott.

clue.text: Lead everybody after mounting skill in old game

indicators.note: mounting means climbing, so in a down entry the word reads upwards

parts.note: art means skill
Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
all means everybody

explanation.surface: Leading everyone in an old sport after climbing up skilfully.
explanation.walkthrough: Lead looks like a verb but is the metal. TRA, the reversed skill word, comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Trapball was an old bat-and-ball game in which the ball was sprung from a trap.

clue.text: Claw, not one found in part of French seaside town

definitions.note: the answer is the second part of La Rochelle

indicators.note: found in means placed inside the next word

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

indicators.note: not one means a letter standing for one is removed

parts.note: a chela is the pincer claw of a crab or lobster

explanation.surface: A crab's claw turns up at a French resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' does double duty: it is the role in the wordplay and also says the answer is only part of the town's name, La Rochelle.
explanation.definitionFit: La Rochelle is a seaport on France's Atlantic coast, so Rochelle forms part of its name.

clue.text: Flowering shrub giving tea flavouring additive in Japan

parts.note: cha is a word for tea
miso is fermented soya paste used to flavour Japanese food

explanation.surface: A shrub's blossoms flavour tea in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: The chamiso is a white-flowered saltbush shrub of the American Southwest.

clue.text: Sir H. Lauder's turn? Not what he'd do round Scots city

indicators.note: not means without, so the letters of the next idea are taken away
round says the letters to be taken away sit on both sides, around what is kept

parts.note: Stirling is a city in central Scotland
Harry Lauder was a music-hall singer, so singing is what he did

explanation.surface: A music-hall star's act is described as something he would never do in a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lauder was a Scottish music-hall singer, so his 'turn' points to a Scots word. S and ING come off either end of STIRLING.
explanation.definitionFit: Tirl is a Scots word for a turn, twirl or spin, so it is how a Scot like Lauder would say turn.

clue.text: Leak I had in pub after samples of real ale (6, two words)

indicators.note: samples are small tastes, so only the opening letters are taken

parts.note: the first letters of real and ale

indicators.note: had in means held inside the next word

parts.note: an inn is a pub
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker admits a leak after sampling the real ale in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Leak looks like a drinker's need after ale, but it is a rain-in, water getting through a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A rain-in is a leak where rain gets through a roof or wall, a Chambers term.

clue.text: King with state requiring relief mostly? It's given as solemn token

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
need is a state of want that calls for relief

explanation.surface: A king whose state badly needs relief.
explanation.walkthrough: To bend the knee, or give the knee, is a solemn token of homage, the sense the definition plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Bending or giving the knee is a formal gesture of respect, fealty or submission.

clue.text: Study re a sect, unusually devoted

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters fall in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A study of a religious sect finds its members unusually devoted.
explanation.definitionFit: To consecrate is to dedicate to a sacred purpose, and consecrate can be an adjective meaning devoted.

clue.text: Growing medium, not old, put out by inventor

indicators.note: something put out is ejected, so those letters are thrown out of the longer word

parts.note: one who coins new words or ideas
ne is an obsolete word for not

explanation.surface: A gardener's new potting compost, cleared of anything old, is thrown out by its inventor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not old' reads as 'new', but it means the archaic word for not, NE, which is removed from COINER to leave COIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Coir, coconut husk fibre, is widely used as a peat-free compost in which plants are grown.

clue.text: Mexican American, one coated in reddish dyestuff

indicators.note: a thing coated in something has that substance all around it on the outside

parts.note: chico, a variant of chica, the orange-red dye from a South American climber
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: Someone of Mexican descent is pictured daubed with red dye.
explanation.walkthrough: Chico is a South American dye, a variant of chica, used by Indigenous peoples to stain the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicano is the term for a US citizen or resident of Mexican descent.

clue.text: Work up composition for tubas around start of concert

indicators.note: around means the instrument letters encircle the extra letter
a composition is something arranged anew, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'start of' keeps only the first letter of 'concert'

parts.note: the first letter of concert

explanation.surface: A brass player works up a piece for tubas to open a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: SUBACT is a rare Chambers word meaning to work up or reduce, as by working soil.
explanation.definitionFit: To subact is to work up thoroughly or subdue, as in working soil or kneading material.

clue.text: It adorned ancient coin or a fresh disc newly minted (10, two words)

indicators.note: something newly minted is freshly made, so the letters are recast in a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An ancient coin, or a freshly struck disc, bears a decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newly minted' suits the coin picture and also signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred fish, worshipped in ancient cults, appeared as emblems stamped on some Greek coins.

clue.text: Jock's rolling wheelie, filled with energy

indicators.note: a container filled with something holds it inside

parts.note: a wheelie bin, a large rubbish bin on wheels
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A wheelie bin rolls along, full of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolling here is 'rolling in it', wealthy; Jock flags a Scots word. A wheelie bin is the British name for a wheeled rubbish bin.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots bien means comfortable or well-off, the sense of being rolling in money.

clue.text: They go up and down on catwalk? Shield men, excited, having day off!

definitions.text: They go up and down on catwalk?

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up and fall into a new order
off means that letter is taken away from the letters given

parts.note: taken as written
D is the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: Men at a fashion show are told to shield themselves, excited and on a day off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on fashion: hemlines rise and fall from season to season, not models walking up and down.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemlines, the lower edges of skirts and dresses, rise and fall with fashion trends shown on the catwalk.

clue.text: Lock cleared of last fish

indicators.note: cleared of last says the final letter is removed

parts.note: Chubb is a well-known brand of lock

explanation.surface: A lock is cleared of the last fish, as if a canal lock were drained.
explanation.walkthrough: Lock suggests a canal, which fits the fish, but it is the Chubb lock brand.
explanation.definitionFit: The chub is a common freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: Metrical measure repetition spoiled — not on

indicators.note: spoiled letters are messed up and rearranged
not here means without, so the following word is taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet's metre is ruined by repetition, which is not on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on' looks like the British idiom for unacceptable, but it tells you to take two letters away before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitrite is a metrical foot of three long syllables and one short, used in classical prosody.

clue.text: Wild and arty, dressed in cheap style

indicators.note: dressed means prepared or arranged, as stone or a salad is dressed, so the letters are set out anew

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wild and arty turns out in gaudy, cheap clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed in' reads as one phrase about clothes, but 'dressed' is the anagram signal and 'in cheap style' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawdrily means in a showy but cheap and tasteless way, especially of dress.

clue.text: Sprinter poorly dressed? We certainly won't pull out

indicators.note: someone dressed in clothes is wrapped inside them

parts.note: rags are poor, shabby clothes
Usain Bolt, the Jamaican sprinter

explanation.surface: A famous sprinter turns up shabbily dressed and says he won't pull out of the race.
explanation.walkthrough: Rag bolts have barbed shanks so that, once set, they cannot be withdrawn; that is the joke in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rag bolt is a jagged bolt designed to grip so it resists being pulled out.

clue.text: Beer knocked back with extremes of excess in feasts

indicators.note: knocked back means turned round, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: lager is a kind of beer
the first and last letters of excess

explanation.surface: Beer is downed with excessive enthusiasm at banquets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' looks like drinking, which suits the beer, but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To regale someone is to entertain them lavishly with food and drink, so feasts works as a verb.

clue.text: Tyro, awfully new, seen getting under wing for cover thereof?

parts.note: an el (ell) is a wing of a building at right angles to the main part

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A novice is seen getting under a wing, looking for cover.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, getting under puts the jumbled letters below EL. 'Wing' serves twice: in the wordplay and as the thing the definition refers to.
explanation.definitionFit: An elytron is a beetle's hardened forewing, which forms a protective sheath over the hind wing.

clue.text: Grand lady, Arabian, needing housemaid around

indicators.note: around means the second word encircles the first

parts.note: bonne is French for a housemaid
Ar is an abbreviation for Arabian or Arabic

explanation.surface: A grand Arabian lady needs her maid around her.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonne is a French word Azed expects the solver to know; the answer is French too, so the whole clue has a French flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: A baronne is a French baroness, a titled noblewoman.

clue.text: Fate? One's limited in preference when there's no ice

indicators.note: something limited in another is confined inside it
no here means without, so the named letters are taken away

parts.note: a choice is a preference
taken as written
one's lot is one's allotted share or fortune

explanation.surface: Is it fate that one's choices are limited when there's no ice?
explanation.walkthrough: One's lot, one's portion in life, echoes the Fate of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Clotho was one of the three Fates of Greek myth, the one who spun the thread of life.

clue.text: Romping oral, with German and English included, first or second? (7, two words)

indicators.note: romping suggests frolicking about, so the letters play around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
W is the abbreviation for with
G is the abbreviation for German
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An oral exam turns into a romp with German and English thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: First and second look like exam grades or places, but they are the gears of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: First and second gear are the low gears of a vehicle, used for starting and slow driving.

clue.text: Purblind Shakespearean failure holding scream back before end of scene

indicators.note: holding means the outer word grips the other letters inside it

parts.note: a dud is a failure

indicators.note: back means the word is written from right to left

parts.note: to yell is to scream

indicators.note: 'end of' keeps only the last letter of 'scene'

parts.note: the last letter of scene

explanation.surface: A failed actor in a Shakespeare play screams backstage at the end of a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock says 'dull-eyed fool' in The Merchant of Venice, hence Shakespearean.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull-eyed means having dim, lacklustre eyes, close to purblind or partly blind, and Shakespeare used it.

clue.text: Neckwear wrapped round rib's head in strong wind

indicators.note: a thing wrapped round another encloses it completely

parts.note: a feather boa is worn round the neck

indicators.note: 'head' keeps only the first letter of 'rib'

parts.note: the first letter of rib

explanation.surface: A scarf wrapped round someone's chest in a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: A bora is a cold north-east wind on the Adriatic.
explanation.definitionFit: The bora is a fierce, cold, gusty wind blowing down onto the Adriatic coast.

clue.text: Dutchwoman, endlessly austere, stuffy one

indicators.note: endlessly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: frow, from Dutch vrouw, a Dutch woman or housewife
stern means austere

explanation.surface: A severe Dutch housewife comes across as a stuffy person.
explanation.walkthrough: Stuffy here is literal: a frowster likes a frowsty, airless room.
explanation.definitionFit: A frowster is someone who enjoys a hot, stuffy, unventilated atmosphere.

clue.text: Seabird with cormorants? Some soaring

indicators.note: soaring means rising, so in a down entry the letters read upwards
some means only part of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters span the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A seabird flies with cormorants, some of them soaring.
explanation.walkthrough: The roch, or rotche, is the little auk.
explanation.definitionFit: The roch is a dialect name for the little auk, a small seabird of the North Atlantic.

clue.text: Black or dim by the sound of it?

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is identified by how it is spoken

parts.note: slow means dim-witted

explanation.surface: Something described as either black or dim, judging by the noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black or dim' reads as a pair of synonyms, but black is the definition and dim is the clue to the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloe can describe the blue-black colour of the blackthorn fruit, as in sloe-black or sloe-eyed.

clue.text: A wee bittie Scotch cheers — something with gin too

parts.note: ta is an informal British thank you
it is Italian vermouth, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: A wee dram of Scotch, a toast, and something to go with the gin too.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin and it is a British cocktail of gin and Italian vermouth, so it partners gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Tait is a Scots word for a small piece or quantity, a wee bit.

clue.text: Nothing held in palm, or tiny amount

indicators.note: held in means placed inside the other word

parts.note: the ita is a South American palm, the miriti
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Holding nothing in the palm of your hand, or very little.
explanation.walkthrough: Palm suggests a hand, but it is the ita palm tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota, the smallest Greek letter, is used for a very small amount, as in 'not one iota'.

clue.text: Precursor for semiconductors aliens manufactured

indicators.note: something manufactured is made from raw material reshaped into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Aliens have manufactured a chemical used in making computer chips.
explanation.definitionFit: Silane gas, silicon hydride, is decomposed to deposit pure silicon in semiconductor manufacture.

clue.text: How-dye-do detected after school

indicators.note: after places the word before it second, behind the following one

parts.note: Sch is the abbreviation for school
take can mean to detect or catch someone out

explanation.surface: A pupil is caught in some mischief after school.
explanation.walkthrough: How-d'ye-do (spelt here with dye) is a fix or predicament, the same as schtook, Yiddish-derived slang for trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A how-d'ye-do is an awkward mess or trouble, which is exactly what being in schtook means.

clue.text: Quarrelsome Scot creating furore, shunned by society

indicators.note: something shunned is kept away, so it is left out

parts.note: to raise a stink is to create a furore
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A Scot who picks fights causes uproar and is shunned by polite society.
explanation.walkthrough: Tink is Scots for a tinker, used for a rough, quarrelsome person.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots a tink is a tinker or a coarse, argumentative person, the kind who starts rows.

clue.text: Poems NY set crafted, generally accessible network (10, two words)

indicators.note: crafted means skilfully made into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Poems set in New York were crafted for everyone to read.
explanation.definitionFit: An open system in computing uses public standards so that it is accessible to and compatible with others.
